title: Leaving Pensacola and New Orleans bands before the boats
summary: He returned from Pensacola, worked with Bebe Ridgley and Lee Collins, turned down Desvigne, then joined the boat.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: How long did you stay in Pensacola?

Oh, I think it was, let's see, I went there in 24, I must have came around about, no, about 20 years, about three years, about 27 years. I said, well, when the job was closed and we left Pensacola, and one stayed in Mobile, and they had a union there. They had a union in Jacksonville. We didn't have no union, black union in New Orleans. And when I was coming back, I told my daddy, this thing was really getting bad. And I, people always taught me, always had something to say, you know. I wrote and told my daddy, I was staying in Mobile, we wouldn't do any much, because the guys that had a union there was blocking us out, see, because we were staying there, didn't mind us coming through, you see. So, he said, come on home, boy. He said, you got, I got a job for you. And the very reason, his brother had got what the man, one of the people, the man that owned, had something to do with the Forsyth Brewery. He had built that place. The blind floor was that door, Rampo Street, they had gambling and restaurant, they built a nice place. And on the second floor was the ballroom dance hall. And the roof garden was still running, and the astroly was still running. We had competition, but he made it. I stayed with that band until Rebair and his brother fell out, and Rebair went back to working in the field, it was for white people. And Emma was in that band all that time. When I went on the boat, that's what I had to. No, I leave Rebair, and when I went to work, I did the dance with Lee Collin. And then when we leave that job, and Beans had a couple of the astroly people, and took over the astroly, not the restaurant part, but the pool table and gambling part, and upstairs. And we had about, I think it was five or six pieces. We had trumpet, sax, double uncrowned it, and David Jones on tenor. And we had four rhythms, seven. And we had the ballyhoo for them. And they'll come Sidney Desby, and he's had trouble with his badge of parade. He come to Alper with me to take the job, and I turned it down. He asked me three times. The third time I took it, because I wanted to see the guy and talk to him. In other words, I'm a guy I don't like to take that from nobody. He said, damn, I can't even remember that name. And another fellow, Don Alper, he had gave me some money, a deposit to build up his band, but I turned him down and gave him his money back. Because I knew the Streck-Food Steemboard people knew that was a good job, you see. And so I left, I leave, after we had made this recording, Randy Hall took the job. He's a very good band to play. He's like me. He studied violin. And he got to be a professor. He's out in California somewhere. He's a very good band. And went on the boat with Sidney Desvene. After work with Sidney Desvene, I worked with the Redford Band and went with the Pudon Band. I was working with the Pudon Band here. He used to play at the Country Club and all the rich white people and everything. Some blacks had a club, you know, or a Sempernore. Used to play there and a couple other places. He used to play up on Lusin Avenue, Virginia Airport, and decided to begin to lot up there. Some white men had decided to have dancing up there. You know what, there was something to do, you know, or things were slow.
